extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators and mathematics education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly survey introducing the questions, methods, and recent developments in the philosophy of mathematical practice, written to inform mathematics educators and researchers about how philosophers study mathematics-as-practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: What are the components of mathematical knowledge?
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical knowledge does not lie solely in theorems; philosophers investigate all the components of mathematical knowledge including proofs, axioms, concepts and definitions, and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the nature of these different components and understand how they function in actual mathematical practice (references: Rav 1999; Detlefsen 2009; Schlimm 2013; Tappenden 2008; Avigad 2006).

rubrics_metrics.name: What do we do when we do mathematics? (human/cognitive agents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is done by human agents; philosophers study how we, as human cognitive agents, actually do mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate roles of visualization, imagination, artefacts (diagrams, notations), and planning agency; integrate empirical results from cognitive science and mathematics education to model mathematical activity (Giaquinto 2007; Muntersbjorn 1999; De Cruz and De Smedt 2013).

rubrics_metrics.name: What is 'good' mathematics?
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify the ways a piece of mathematics can be considered 'good' beyond mere correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mathematics on values such as explanatory power, beauty, purity, depth, fruitfulness, fittingness, interestingness, and motivation; assess 'good' mathematical design (notations, structure) and how mathematics should be structured (Steiner 1978; Rota 1997; Avigad 2020; De Toffoli 2017).

rubrics_metrics.name: In what sense is mathematics a social practice?
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical practice is inherently social; philosophers examine mathematics' social dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study peer review, journals, conferences, collaborative theorem-proving, social values and norms, and how social practices shape mathematical knowledge and standards (Löwe and Müller 2010; Ferreirós 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: What can the history of mathematics tell us about its nature?
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical case studies are used to understand changes in mathematics and their consequences for its nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine historical and philosophical approaches to analyze changes in practices, concepts, and methods across time (Manders 2008; Avigad and Morris 2014, 2016; Ferreirós 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: What is the relationship between mathematics and other disciplines?
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate how mathematics relates to and is used in other disciplines and what this reveals about mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze relationships with fields like computer science, physics, biology, and study applicability to the external world (Avigad 2008a, Urquhart 2008a/b, Islami and Longo 2017, Pincock 2012).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case studies (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of analyzing in detail one or more phenomena in the context of specific mathematical practice, past or present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often exploratory but usually directed at special issues; can be used to support or provide counterexamples to conceptual analyses or frameworks; widely employed across topics (e.g., diagrams, proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual analysis (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Answering 'What is X?' by reflecting on our understanding of a concept, typically formulating necessary and sufficient conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to analyze values (e.g., what it means for a proof to be explanatory, beautiful, deep, fruitful, etc.); appropriate where concepts admit clear analytic conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual frameworks (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing a broader network of notions and theses when phenomena do not lend themselves to piecemeal conceptual analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct whole frameworks to characterize notions like 'mathematical practice' (examples: Kitcher 1984; Van Bendegem & Van Kerkhove 2004; Ferreirós 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing reasoned arguments for and against particular philosophical views within the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support a view by showing it (i) accounts for a wide range of cases, (ii) aligns with mathematical practice, and/or (iii) relies on minimal assumptions; argue against a view via counterexamples, unwanted consequences, or exposing problematic assumptions (examples cited throughout).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Using empirical tools (interviews, psychological experiments, surveys) borrowed from social sciences, cognitive science, and mathematics education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in interdisciplinary research to study peer review, how mathematicians write papers, evaluations of proofs, knowledge ascriptions, online mathematical discussions, and cognitive bases of diagrammatic reasoning (Geist et al. 2010; Inglis & Aberdein 2014; Pease et al. 2019; Hamami et al. submitted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imports from other fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopting concepts, models, or techniques from other disciplines to analyze mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: formal verification models for value judgments and understanding, modularity from software engineering to analyze mathematical knowledge structure, cognitive-science findings for visual thinking (Avigad 2006/2008/2020; Giaquinto 2007).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal proof (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal proof is specified relative to a given formal deductive system (a triple of formal language L, axioms A, and rules of inference R); a formal proof is a sequence of formulas each an axiom or the result of applying a rule to previous formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notion constitutes a normative account of what a proof ought to be and has also been taken as a descriptive account of what proofs are in practice; distinction between its syntactic character and informal proofs' semantic/intuitive aspects is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features distinguishing informal proofs (Rav)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal proofs possess features not captured by formal proofs: (1) 'irreducible semantic content' lost in translation to formal proofs; (2) the catalyzing role of informal proofs in the growth of mathematical knowledge (development of tools, methods, concepts); (3) capacity of informal proofs to serve as vehicles for know-how (methodologies, strategies, systematisation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features motivate philosophical accounts of proofs faithful to practice and emphasize epistemic importance of informal proofs beyond theorems they establish (Rav 1999).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of informal proofs via informal logic and proof-dialogues (Aberdein)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal proofs can be analyzed using informal logic by taking into account their dialogical context and different types of 'proof dialogues'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes role of conversational context (Walton) and categorizes dialogical roles that informal proofs play in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal proofs possess semantic and intuitive dimensions (Leitgeb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal proofs differ from formal proofs in having a semantic dimension (terms/sentences are interpreted) and an intuitive dimension (elementary steps and axioms are taken to be intuitive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dimensions explain resistance of informal proofs to formal translation and the role of intuition in mathematical practice (Leitgeb 2009).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal proofs as inferential actions on non-propositional representations (Larvor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences in informal proofs should be conceived as inferential actions acting on not only propositions but also diagrams, notational expressions, physical/mental/computer models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many inferential actions depend on domain-specific representations they resist formal translation; account helps explain loss when informal proofs are recast formally (Larvor 2012).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor of mathematical proofs (Burgess)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor is 'the quality whose presence in a purported proof makes it a genuine proof by present-day journal standards, and whose absence makes the proof spurious in a way that, if discovered, will call for retraction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One common answer equates rigor with routinary translatability into a formal proof (the 'standard view'), but this is contested; an account of rigor should align with how mathematicians judge proofs in ordinary practice (Burgess 2015; critiques by Marfori, Detlefsen, Tanswell, Larvor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of visualization and artefacts in mathematical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual representations (internal imagery and external artefacts like diagrams, symbolic systems, notations, computer images) play important roles in proving, discovering, explaining, justifying, and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to received nineteenth-century dismissals, arguments defend a positive epistemic role for pictures/diagrams (Brown, Giaquinto); visual thinking is diverse across domains and requires a fine-grained taxonomy; empirical and case-study methods are commonly used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manders' co-exact vs exact attributes for Euclidean diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish co-exact attributes (insensitive to a range of continuous deformations of a diagram) from exact attributes (sensitive and obtaining only in isolated cases); Euclid's diagram-based attributions are limited to co-exact attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because co-exact attributes are stable under concrete drawing, diagrams can be reliably used for certain attributions; exact attributes must be established via demonstration text rather than read off the diagram (Manders 2008).
